FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt
A 700MW cross-border transmission line will bring affordable power to the DRC's Copperbelt, unlock new mining and industrial capacity, open export routes for licensed Zambian power producers, and enable new generation.
FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt.
FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt
A 700MW cross-border transmission line will bring affordable power to the DRC's Copperbelt, unlock new mining and industrial capacity, open export routes for licensed Zambian power producers, and enable new generation
Published on
6 Oct 2026
Kinshasa, 6 October 2026 – The Strategic Investment Fund of the Democratic Republic of the Congo ("FIS-RDC"), Enterprise Power DRC SARL ("EnPower"), Trafigura and Gridworks Development Partners (together, "the Parties") have signed a Strategic Framework Agreement to jointly finance, build and operate a 200km high-voltage power line connecting Kalumbila, Zambia, with Kolwezi, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The Kalumbila–Kolwezi Interconnector Project ("KKIP") will strengthen the DRC's connection to the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), the regional body that links national grids and allows countries to trade power across borders. The project has reached the final stage of development, with all necessary concessions, licences and authorisations secured. It has an estimated construction cost of USD300 million.
KKIP will deliver benefits on both sides of the border: a new source of reliable, affordable power for the DRC's mining and industrial sectors, and new export capacity and transmission opportunities for Zambian power producers. The line will have a thermal capacity of 700MW, enabling up to 550MW of competitively priced electricity to be imported into the Copperbelt mining region of the DRC. The line design allows for a future capacity increase to over 1GW.
The Parties and financing
FIS-RDC, EnPower and Gridworks have confirmed their intention to invest equity in KKIP, with Gridworks as lead equity investor and majority shareholder. The Parties are in discussions with Zambian entities about taking a stake in the project. EnPower is the project developer, a licensed Congolese power trader and a SAPP member. Gridworks is a specialist transmission and distribution developer owned and funded by British International Investment, the UK Government’s development finance institution. Trafigura, a market leader in the global commodities industry, has agreed to arrange a significant share of the project's debt financing.
For FIS-RDC, the transaction supports the DRC Government's objective of investing in strategic infrastructure with wider economic benefits. It is the first investment announced by FIS-RDC since its creation in October 2025.
Benefits for the DRC
KKIP will help address the country's structural energy deficit of more than 1GW. It is expected to:
Supply electricity from across Southern Africa to power Congolese mining and industry, supporting social and economic development in local communities.
Enable the development of mining and refining projects currently on hold due to a lack of available, cost-effective baseload power.
Increase mining and refining output, generating greater fiscal contributions for the DRC.
Deliver broader benefits for the DRC by expanding access to reliable, affordable power for communities and businesses, supporting local enterprise and jobs, and contributing to economic diversification.
Benefits for Zambia
KKIP will create export opportunities for Zambian power producers, provide transmission capacity for licensed operators, and help spur the development of new generation. The participation of FIS-RDC, alongside Gridworks and Trafigura, will also strengthen cooperation between the DRC and Zambian governments and create a platform for long-term investment. Discussions are already underway with Zambian entities on potential co-investment.
Emile Osumba, CEO of FIS-RDC, said: "KKIP is the Fund's inaugural transaction, and it reflects precisely the mandate entrusted to us by the Government. By helping close the Copperbelt's power deficit, the project will unlock industrial growth, skilled jobs and fiscal revenue for the DRC. By backing a project led by a private Congolese developer, FIS-RDC is demonstrating that sovereign capital can act as a catalyst for private investment rather than a substitute for it. And by co-investing alongside credible and experienced partners such as Gridworks, we are building the track record that will allow the Fund to mobilise further capital for the country's strategic infrastructure."
Marc Orphanides, Managing Director of EnPower, added: “This agreement is an important milestone towards executing this strategic transmission infrastructure, which will add significant capacity to meet the ever-growing power demand of the DRC mining industry. We are grateful to the authorities, stakeholders and communities in the DRC and Zambia, as well as the International Finance Corporation, for their support to KKIP, which will be the first privately developed and financed cross-border transmission infrastructure on the African continent.”
Gonzalo De Olazaval, Global Head of Metals and Minerals at Trafigura, commented: “Trafigura is proud to support this landmark power project in the DRC, part of our broader power strategy in Africa. Reliable, competitively priced power is a critical enabler of economic growth across the continent, and Trafigura is well placed to bring together the investment, infrastructure and partnerships needed to make these projects a reality. KKIP has the potential to unlock industrial growth in the DRC and Zambia, while also supporting job creation and local communities in both countries.”
Chris Flavin, CEO of Gridworks, said: “Gridworks is proud to be the lead equity investor in KKIP. This is an important regional integration project. Zambia and the DRC both stand to benefit from closer interconnection, and this project will give the Copperbelt access to reliable, competitively priced power and lay the foundation for further cross-border transmission investment across Southern Africa. While the project is anchored by mining offtake, there is capacity on the line to serve the wider population too. Connecting regional power markets and supporting efficient energy trading is key to sustained economic growth in the region. We look forward to working alongside our partners to deliver this important infrastructure."

articles.title: Philippines grants 30-day visa-free entry to South Africa, Kenya, the US and 44 other African countries, but leaves out Nigeria, China and India - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Philippines grants 30-day visa-free entry to South Africa, Kenya, the US and 44 other African countries, but leaves out Nigeria, China and India  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- The Philippines now allows citizens of 46 African countries to enter visa-free for up to 30 days to boost tourism and investment.
- Travellers must have a passport valid for at least six months and a return or onward ticket to qualify.
- China and India are excluded from the general 30-day visa-free policy; Chinese visitors have up to 14 days visa-free with different rules.
- Tourists can extend their stay by 29 days for a total of 59 days, while the visa-free entry list covers 157 countries overall, with some special cases.
The Philippines is allowing citizens of 46 African countries, including South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, Uganda and Tanzania, to enter visa-free for up to 30 days, alongside travellers from the US, UK, Canada and Japan, while Nigeria, China and India remain outside the standard arrangement.
Under Executive Order No. 408 and subsequent amendments, eligible travellers must hold passports valid for at least six months beyond their planned stay and have a return or onward ticket.
African countries covered by the policy include South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Morocco, Rwanda, Senegal, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Other eligible countries include Benin, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Cape Verde, Central African Republic, Chad, Comoros, Republic of Congo, Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea and Eritrea.
Gabon, Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, São Tomé and Príncipe, Seychelles, Eswatini, Togo and Tunisia also qualify.
However, nationals of Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan do not qualify for the Philippines’ standard 30-day visa-free entry and generally require a visa before travelling.
China and India, two of Asia’s largest economies, are also outside the arrangement, although both benefit from separate visa-free rules with shorter stays.
By contrast, citizens of major economies including the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Japan, Germany, France and South Korea qualify for the 30-day visa-free arrangement.
Philippines targets more foreign visitors
The visa policy comes as Manila seeks to strengthen tourism’s contribution to the economy and make the country more accessible to overseas visitors.
The Philippines recorded about 5.94 million international tourists in 2025, while inbound visitor spending reached an estimated 694 billion Philippine pesos. Tourism contributed 8.1% to the economy and supported about 7.7 million jobs during the year.
International arrivals have continued to rise in 2026, with the government also pushing for better airports, transport links and international connectivity.
Tourism Secretary Dita Angara-Mathay said the government wants to show that the Philippines is “open, accessible, and ready for greater tourism and investment.”
Longer stays are possible
Travellers admitted under the 30-day visa-free arrangement can apply for an initial 29-day extension through the Philippine Bureau of Immigration, taking their authorised stay to 59 days.
The broader visa-free list covers 157 countries, although separate rules apply to some nationalities. Brazilian and Israeli passport holders, for instance, can enter visa-free for up to 59 days under existing bilateral agreements.

articles.summary: China Railway Construction Engineering Pivots to Tanzania Dira 2050 Vision After Decades of Infrastructure Development  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
The strategic pivot was highlighted at the Phoenix Global Development Forum for Enterprises in Dar es Salaam, where government officials, business leaders, and academics convened to map the next phase of Sino-Tanzanian economic cooperation. For CRJE, the forum marked a transition from historical aid-driven projects to modern, commercial infrastructure development aligned with Tanzania's long-term economic blueprint.
From TAZARA to Modern Infrastructure
The company's Tanzanian footprint dates back to 1969, when its parent group, China Railway Construction Engineering Group (CRCEG), dispatched 1,114 employees to participate in the construction of TAZARA. This monumental infrastructure project was designed to link landlocked Zambia's copper belt to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam, bypassing routes controlled by apartheid-era regimes in southern Africa.
During the initial construction phase, the Chinese team undertook approximately 506,400 square meters of building works along the railway line. This extensive effort included the construction of 93 stations, locomotive and rolling stock repair plants, technical training schools, depots, hospitals, and accommodation facilities. The project not only transformed regional logistics but also established a deep cultural and technical exchange between the two nations.
After TAZARA became operational, CRCEG retained a specialized team to undertake ongoing maintenance work along the railway corridor. The company formally registered its Tanzanian branch in Dar es Salaam in 2000, coinciding with the country's launch of Vision 2025. In 2013, as its business portfolio expanded beyond rail, the entity was rebranded as CRJE (East Africa) Limited, reflecting its broader mandate in the regional construction market.
Aligning with Dira 2050
Tanzania's newly articulated National Development Vision 2050, popularly known as Dira 2050, demands massive upgrades in transport, energy, and urban infrastructure to achieve middle-to-high-income economic status. The Phoenix Global Development Forum, co-organized by Phoenix TV and the Chinese Enterprises Association in Tanzania (CEAT), provided a platform for CRJE to outline its aspirations for this next developmental chapter.
The forum was attended by high-profile figures, including Minister of State in the President's Office for Planning and Investment, Prof Kitila Mkumbo, and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Resident Representative Shigeki Komatsubara. Their presence underscored the institutional importance placed on foreign direct investment and public-private partnerships in realizing the nation's mid-century goals.
For CRJE, the transition to Dira 2050 involves moving beyond traditional civil works to encompass complex, technology-driven infrastructure projects. This includes modern port expansions, smart city developments, and large-scale irrigation schemes designed to support Tanzania's rapidly growing population and agricultural export ambitions. The company views its historical presence as a unique competitive advantage, offering institutional memory and established government relations that newer market entrants lack.
The Evolution of Sino-Tanzanian Cooperation
The trajectory of CRJE mirrors the broader evolution of Sino-African economic relations. In the 1970s, projects like TAZARA were primarily state-led aid initiatives, funded by concessional loans and driven by geopolitical solidarity. Today, the partnership is characterized by commercial contracts, joint ventures, and a focus on mutual economic benefit.
A critical component of this modern partnership is technology transfer and local capacity building. Echoing the technical training schools established during the TAZARA era, CRJE now emphasizes the employment and upskilling of Tanzanian engineers and project managers. This approach not only reduces operational costs but also fosters local goodwill and ensures that the technical expertise required to maintain complex infrastructure remains within the country.
Challenges and Future Prospects
Despite its deep roots, CRJE operates in an increasingly competitive and scrutinized market. Tanzanian authorities are placing greater emphasis on debt sustainability, environmental compliance, and the use of local subcontractors. International financial institutions and domestic civil society organizations frequently demand greater transparency regarding the terms of infrastructure financing and the long-term economic viability of mega-projects.
Furthermore, the company must navigate the complexities of Tanzania's evolving regulatory environment, which seeks to maximize local content and ensure that foreign investments translate into tangible job creation and skills development. As Tanzania pushes toward its mid-century economic goals, CRJE's evolution from a railway builder to a comprehensive infrastructure partner reflects the maturing, complex nature of foreign direct investment in East Africa. The success of this transition will depend on the firm's ability to balance commercial imperatives with the developmental priorities of its host nation.
Industry observers note that the next decade will be critical for CRJE as it competes against both Western contractors and other Asian firms for lucrative government tenders. To maintain its market leadership, the firm is increasingly integrating green building practices and renewable energy components into its project proposals, aligning with global climate finance requirements. Ultimately, CRJE's continued relevance in Tanzania will be measured not just by the volume of concrete poured, but by its contribution to sustainable, inclusive economic growth under the Dira 2050 framework.

articles.title: 81% African businesses expect rise in economic activities despite AfCFTA hurdles: PAFTRAC - Peoples Gazette Nigeria
articles.summary: 81% African businesses expect rise in economic activities despite AfCFTA hurdles: PAFTRAC  Peoples Gazette Nigeria
articles.full_text:
81% African businesses expect rise in economic activities despite AfCFTA hurdles: PAFTRAC
African businesses expect their cross-border transaction activities to increase significantly over the next 12 months despite challenges in implementing the African Continental Free Trade Area, according to a report by the Pan African Private Sector Trade and Investment Committee (PAFTRAC).
According to PAFTRAC, its ‘Africa CEO Trade Survey,’ presented recently at the World Trade Organisation Public Forum in Geneva, Switzerland, found that 81.3 per cent of senior executives surveyed expect their cross-border economic activity to increase over the next 12 months.
A total of 2,500 business leaders were surveyed for the study, with four in five respondents saying they expect the increase. Now in its sixth year, the PAFTRAC survey started with 400 respondents in 2021 and the number grew steadily to 2,500 participants in 2026.
“African Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) express optimism, but credit risk and policy gaps hinder intra-African trade. PAFTRAC’s survey of 2,500 business leaders reveals that four in five expect their cross-border activity to increase over the next twelve months, despite AfCFTA implementation hurdles and financing constraints,” the group said on Tuesday.
It added, “The survey, now in its sixth year and expanded from 400 respondents in 2021 to over 2,500 in 2026, is the most robust barometer of African executive sentiment on trade available. Its findings point to a continent where the appetite for regional integration is outpacing the systems designed to enable it.”
Despite the optimistic outlook, PAFTRAC said access to finance remains a key challenge for African countries, noting that sovereign and institutional borrowers across the continent continue to receive risk assessments from Western credit agencies that, according to IFC estimates cited by the committee, add about $31 billion in extra borrowing costs each year.
“A total of 57 per cent of the executives surveyed described access to trade finance for cross-border transactions as difficult or very difficult. The IFC estimates Africa’s SME financing gap at more than $331 billion,” PAFTRAC stated.
Commenting on the report, Chairperson of PAFTRAC, Patrick Utomi, described perception of Africa by Western credit agencies as a “prejudice premium.”
He added, “When capital is priced so that an economy actively at war receives more competitive financing than a stable, peaceful African sovereign, the system is misreading reality. Outdated global rules and subjective rating methodologies are imposing a direct tax on African trade.”

articles.title: Kenya Pushes for Accelerated AfCFTA Implementation at Alamein Forum - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Kenya Pushes for Accelerated AfCFTA Implementation at Alamein Forum  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Kenya has called for an immediate acceleration in the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), urging member states to dismantle non-tariff barriers that continue to stifle intra-continental commerce.
Speaking at the inaugural Alamein Africa Business Forum and the 8th African Union Mid-Year Coordination Meeting in Egypt, Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi argued that regional integration must yield tangible economic dividends for ordinary citizens rather than remaining a bureaucratic exercise.
Dismantling Trade Barriers
Mudavadi, representing President William Ruto at the high-level diplomatic gathering, emphasized that the secure movement of African businesspeople, investors, and professionals is a prerequisite for the continent's economic liberation. He noted that while tariff reductions have been negotiated, hidden bureaucratic hurdles at border points still impose severe costs on regional supply chains.
“Africa’s integration must be felt beyond conference rooms, in the markets our businesses access, the jobs our young people secure and the opportunities our citizens can pursue across borders,” Mudavadi stated during his keynote address. The Prime Cabinet Secretary highlighted that faster implementation of the AfCFTA protocol would translate directly into wider markets for Kenyan manufactured goods and agricultural exports.
Trade analysts have long pointed out that non-tariff barriers, including arbitrary customs checks, divergent sanitary standards, and restrictive visa regimes, cost African economies billions of dollars annually. By prioritizing the free movement of persons and capital, Kenya is positioning itself as the primary logistics and financial hub for the East African Community and the broader continental market.
Strengthening Continental Institutions
Beyond trade, the Nairobi delegation welcomed the forum’s declaration aimed at strengthening coordination among African Union institutions and Regional Economic Communities. The agreement seeks to eliminate institutional duplication, a chronic challenge that has historically slowed the execution of continental commitments like Agenda 2063.
Mudavadi stressed that an integrated Africa must also be a peaceful and competitive bloc capable of negotiating favorable terms in global markets. He linked economic prosperity directly to regional stability, noting that investors require predictable security environments to commit long-term capital to cross-border infrastructure and manufacturing projects.
The coordination meeting also reviewed the 2026 agreement on the African Standby Force, a critical mechanism for rapid, African-led peace operations. Kenya’s endorsement of the framework underscores its commitment to resolving regional conflicts through multilateral structures rather than relying on external military interventions, which often come with conditionalities that undermine sovereignty.
The Geopolitics of African Trade
The Alamein forum, hosted by Egypt, comes at a time when global supply chains are fragmenting due to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Eastern Europe. African leaders are increasingly leveraging these disruptions to position the continent as a reliable alternative manufacturing and energy hub.
However, the realization of this vision depends heavily on domestic policy alignment. Member states must harmonize their national industrial policies with continental frameworks to prevent a race to the bottom on labor and environmental standards. The AfCFTA Secretariat has repeatedly warned that without robust dispute resolution mechanisms, larger economies could dominate smaller ones, exacerbating regional inequalities.
Kenya’s push for faster implementation also aligns with its domestic agenda to expand export processing zones and attract foreign direct investment into special economic zones along the Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia Transport corridor. By securing preferential access to a market of over 1.4 billion people, Nairobi aims to offset the declining margins in traditional Western export markets.
Next Steps for Regional Integration
As the coordination meeting concluded, delegations committed to establishing binding timelines for the removal of specific non-tariff barriers identified by the private sector. The success of these commitments will be measured by the volume of intra-African trade over the next four quarters, a metric that currently hovers below 15 percent of the continent's total commercial exchanges.
For Kenyan entrepreneurs and regional logistics firms, the diplomatic assurances from Alamein offer a glimpse of a more frictionless trading environment. Yet, the transition from political declarations to enforced customs protocols remains the ultimate test of Africa’s integration ambitions. The continent's economic future now depends on the political will to enforce the very agreements its leaders have signed.

articles.title: Fuel imports, rising prices squeeze Ghana’s trade surplus – GSS - CitiNewsroom.com
articles.summary: Fuel imports, rising prices squeeze Ghana’s trade surplus – GSS  CitiNewsroom.com
articles.full_text:
Ghana’s growing reliance on fuel imports is putting increasing pressure on the country’s trade balance, with fuel and mineral products accounting for about 30% of total imports in the second quarter of 2026.
The Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) Quarterly Trade Statistics shows diesel, or gas oil, was the country’s largest single import during the period, valued at GH¢12.2 billion, while super petrol imports amounted to another GH¢8 billion.
The development contributed to a sharp increase in Ghana’s import bill, which rose by 47.5% in the second quarter compared with the first quarter.
Fuel costs drive imports
The GSS says fuel imports remain particularly vulnerable to movements in international prices.
Import prices increased by 22.7% during the quarter, while fuel import prices alone surged by 54.1%.
The higher import costs contributed to a significant narrowing of Ghana’s trade surplus, which fell by 70.1% from GH¢46.1 billion in the first quarter to GH¢13.8 billion in the second quarter.
Gold supports export earnings
The GSS is also cautioning that Ghana’s headline trade surplus remains heavily supported by high export prices, particularly gold, rather than broad-based growth in export volumes.
This leaves the country exposed to external price shocks and highlights the vulnerability created by a narrow export base.
The Service is therefore calling for measures to diversify Ghana’s exports, increase local processing and value addition, and expand access to international markets.
It is also recommending stronger implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), improved transport and border infrastructure, and better access to financing for exporters.
According to the GSS, reducing dependence on a narrow range of exports while strengthening domestic production and processing will be critical to building a more resilient trade position and reducing Ghana’s exposure to global price movements.

articles.title: Tinubu commits to 20 per cent manufacturing GDP by 2030 - The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.summary: Tinubu commits to 20 per cent manufacturing GDP by 2030  The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.full_text:
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has committed to raising manufacturing’s contribution to gross domestic product (GDP) to between 20 and 25 per cent by 2030, pledging increased access to power, credit, raw materials and markets to drive the expansion.
Tinubu, who spoke yesterday through the Minister of State for Industry, Trade and Investment, John Owan Enoh, at the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria’s (MAN) 54th yearly general meeting held in Lagos, said the target could not be achieved through policy documents alone.
He said manufacturing’s contribution to real GDP fell from 9.57 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 to 7.72 per cent in the second quarter, even as manufacturing output grew by 3.29 per cent and 3.24 per cent, respectively.
“It will be reached by power in your plans, by credit in your accounts, by raw materials at your gates and markets for your goods,” he said.
Tinubu said the government’s industrial policy envisaged channelling up to five per cent of GDP into industrial financing, adding that implementation would be driven by seven strategic thrusts.
He said the Industrial Revolution Work Group, chaired by Enoh, brings government, the organised private sector, financiers and development partners together under a common scorecard.
The scorecard, he said, would measure progress by factories reopened, capacity utilisation, jobs created, exports shipped and new factories established.
The President also said he had directed the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, through the Industrial Revolution Work Group, to hold quarterly delivery dialogues with MAN.
According to him, the dialogue would enable the association to hold the government accountable for implementation of the industrial policy.
On financing, Tinubu said the government would work with the Bank of Industry, development finance institutions and commercial banks to provide patient, affordable and long-term funding for productive enterprises.
He also said the government would continue to prioritise gas for industry and reliable electricity for industrial clusters, while public procurement would favour Nigerian-made goods that meet required standards under the Nigeria First policy.
He added that industrial corridors, highways and supply routes would be protected, while trade facilitation measures, including the National Single Window, would reduce the time and cost of moving goods across ports and borders.
Tinubu said Nigeria must position itself to take advantage of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which he described as a single market of 1.4 billion people with a combined GDP of about $3.4 trillion.
He noted that only 3.4 per cent of Nigeria’s non-oil exports in 2025 went to fellow ECOWAS member states, describing Africa as the largest market Nigeria was yet to fully serve.
“Nigeria will not be Africa’s warehouse storing what others make. Nigeria will be Africa’s workshop making what Africa needs and sending it with pride across the continent and beyond,” he said.
He urged manufacturers to invest in capacity, deepen backward integration, meet the standards of target markets, train and retain young people, and regard the African market as their home market.
Tinubu also said MAN estimated that manufacturers’ unsold inventory stood at just under N2 trillion, with some companies selling below production cost to keep their factories operating.
MAN President, Francis Meshioye, said the successful implementation of the Nigeria Industrial Policy would depend on consistency, institutional coordination and measurable outcomes.
He said progress should be assessed through improved industrial competitiveness, lower production costs, increased investment in productive capacity, stronger manufacturing exports, greater participation in regional and global value chains, and higher industrial employment.
Meshioye said manufactured goods accounted for only N2.5 trillion, or 2.94 per cent, of Nigeria’s total exports of N85.13 trillion in 2025.
He said MAN considered implementation of the National Industrial Policy central to improving the operating environment for manufacturers and strengthening Nigeria’s industrial base.
Meshioye urged the Federal Government to fast-track implementation of the policy, with clearly defined timelines, measurable performance indicators and institutional accountability across relevant ministries, departments and agencies.
He also called for the establishment of a Nigeria First Industrial Fund to provide long-term concessionary financing, support technology upgrading and promote local value addition.

articles.title: Ethiopia’s export earnings surge to record $11.2 billion as currency reforms take hold - Businessfront
articles.summary: Ethiopia’s export earnings surge to record $11.2 billion as currency reforms take hold  Businessfront
articles.full_text:
Ethiopia recorded export earnings of 11.2 billion US dollars in its latest fiscal year — an unprecedented level of revenue that the government attributes to sweeping reforms to its foreign-exchange regime and broader economic restructuring.
President Taye Atske Selassie disclosed the figures on Tuesday while addressing a joint opening session of the House of Peoples’ Representatives and the House of Federation, Ethiopia’s bicameral parliament, where he outlined the government’s economic, political, and social priorities for the new fiscal year.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows reached 4.5 billion US dollars over the same period, Taye said, while the manufacturing sector expanded by 15.8 percent. Total domestic revenue came in at nearly 1.98 trillion birr, and credit supplied to the economy rose to 1.3 trillion birr.
The president presented the results as evidence that the economy had continued to expand despite domestic and external pressures — a notable claim for a country that has navigated internal conflict, regional instability, and the aftershocks of global commodity and currency volatility in recent years.
Agriculture drives the headline numbers
Agriculture emerged as a central pillar of the growth story. Annual crop production rose from around 335 million quintals seven years ago to 1.3 billion quintals in the 2025/26 fiscal year — a near-fourfold increase that the government cited as a major driver of export revenue growth, though no specific export sectors or commodities were named in the address.
Ethiopia is one of Africa’s largest agricultural economies, with coffee, sesame, and cut flowers among its historically significant export earners. The scale of the crop production increase suggests productivity gains across a broad base of the sector rather than a single commodity surge.
Inflation still a concern, but easing
Meanwhile, inflation declined to 13.4 percent as of May 2026, down from higher levels in preceding periods. The government has set a target of bringing the rate into single digits during the current fiscal year — an ambition that will test the durability of the macroeconomic stabilisation measures introduced alongside the foreign-exchange reforms.
Ethiopia liberalised its foreign-exchange market in 2024, allowing the birr to trade at market-determined rates after decades of a managed peg. The move was a condition of International Monetary Fund support and was designed to close the gap between the official and parallel exchange rates, attract foreign investment, and boost export competitiveness.
The record export figure and the rise in FDI suggest those reforms are beginning to produce measurable results, though inflation remaining above 13 percent indicates that the adjustment process is not yet complete.
Taye’s address came a day after Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was reappointed for another term as Ethiopia entered a new parliamentary cycle. The administration said it would seek to build on current gains by expanding exports, improving productivity, attracting additional foreign investment, and strengthening domestic revenue mobilisation.
For investors and trade partners engaged across East Africa, Ethiopia’s trajectory carries regional weight: as the continent’s second most populous country and a major logistics and manufacturing hub, its economic performance has downstream implications for supply chains, regional trade flows, and investment appetite across the Horn of Africa.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Manufactured Exports Stagnant At 2.94% Despite N85trn Export Surge - LEADERSHIP Newspapers
articles.summary: Nigeria’s Manufactured Exports Stagnant At 2.94% Despite N85trn Export Surge  LEADERSHIP Newspapers
articles.full_text:
The president of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), Otunba Francis Meshioye, said Nigeria’s industrial value addition remains weak, with manufactured exports accounting for only 2.94 per cent of total exports in 2025 despite overall export growth.
Meshioye spoke on Tuesday at the 6th Adeola Odutola Lecture and Presidential Luncheon of the 54th Annual General Meeting of MAN held in Lagos.
The AGM was themed ‘Leveraging National Industrial Policy to Position Nigeria as Africa’s Industrial Hub’.
According to data from the National Bureau of Statistics cited by Meshioye, Nigeria’s total exports rose to N85.13 trillion in 2025, yet manufactured exports stood at only N2.50 trillion.
“This tells us something important: Nigeria is exporting more, but industrial value addition is not expanding at the pace required to transform the economy,” he said.
He noted that despite growth in overall export earnings, the share of manufactured exports has remained broadly unchanged over the past four years, underscoring dependence on primary commodity exports.
Meshioye said if Nigeria must become Africa’s industrial hub, it must build productive capacity that enables Nigerian firms to compete across Africa and globally under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
He commended President Bola Tinubu for launching the Nigeria Industrial Policy 2025 (NIP 2025), describing it as a landmark policy providing strategic opportunity to accelerate industrial development, strengthen domestic value chains, enhance productivity and attract investment.
He thanked the administration for allowing MAN to contribute to developing the policy and reaffirmed the association’s commitment to its successful implementation.
Meshioye warned that the significance of NIP 2025 depends on consistent implementation, institutional coordination and measurable outcomes.
He listed seven structural constraints confronting manufacturers: inadequacy and high cost of power, low contribution of manufacturing to exports, high cost of production inputs and logistics, weak protection against unfair trade practices, policy and regulatory uncertainty, inadequate infrastructure, and skills, technology and innovation gaps.
“These challenges are interconnected. They are compounded by cumulative cost of taxes and regulatory compliance, limited access to long-term industrial finance, weak domestic value chains and dependence on imported inputs,” he added.
He urged federal government to fast-track implementation of NIP 2025 with clear timelines, performance indicators and institutional accountability, and to empower the Industrial Revolution Working Group to coordinate reforms.
He also called for establishment of a Nigeria First Industrial Fund to provide long-term concessionary financing, review of industrial electricity pricing, accelerated provision of reliable power including dedicated industrial feeders, and strengthening of foreign exchange support for productive manufacturers.

Egypt is seeking to deepen economic and industrial ties with South Africa by expanding industrial integration, developing joint projects and attracting new investments in key sectors, Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem stated on Monday.
Hashem's remarks came during a meeting with South African Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition Mpho Parks Tau on October 5, 2026, to discuss ways to strengthen industrial cooperation and build on the outcomes of the African Automotive Investment Forum held in El Alamein.
Egypt's minister said Cairo is keen to strengthen economic and industrial relations with Pretoria, describing the two countries as having longstanding ties and a history of economic cooperation based on mutual interests.
He said the Ministry of Industry is working to maximize the use of available resources and capabilities in both countries to establish joint projects, increase the added value of raw materials and enhance the competitiveness of Egyptian and South African products.
Hashem identified pharmaceuticals, automotive manufacturing and feeder industries, agro-processing, metal industries, infrastructure and logistics zones as key areas offering potential for expanded cooperation.
Focus on Automotive Industry
Hashem affirmed Egypt’s keenness to attract global automotive manufacturers and component producers to establish production facilities in the country, helping meet domestic demand while supporting exports to international markets.
He noted that Egypt has taken steps to deepen the localization of automotive components and attract major international companies to invest in sectors including automotive tires and electric vehicle batteries.
The minister also highlighted opportunities for cooperation between Egypt and South Africa in testing and certifying vehicles and automotive components.
Such cooperation, he said, could facilitate trade and strengthen industrial integration between the two countries and across African markets, while helping products manufactured in Egypt and South Africa gain wider access to continental markets.
Steel, Manganese Cooperation
The talks also covered the possibility of establishing joint projects in iron and steel and manganese alloys, which are important inputs for heavy industries.
Hashem said such projects could help both countries make better use of their mineral resources while increasing the value of raw materials before they enter production chains, in line with Egypt’s industrial strategy.
In turn, Tau reaffirmed South Africa’s interest in expanding cooperation with Egypt in automotive manufacturing and components, as well as identifying additional areas for industrial and investment partnerships that could benefit both economies.
He pointed to the African Automotive Investment Forum, recently held in El Alamein, as an important platform for advancing cooperation between the two countries.
Tau noted that the forum resulted in several agreements, including a partnership between Egypt’s El Araby Group and South African company Malben Engineering to establish a joint industrial platform for manufacturing automotive components.
The two sides also inked a protocol to launch the Egyptian-South African Business Council.
Tau described the agreements as an initial step toward broader industrial and investment cooperation, saying they could pave the way for additional partnerships between Egyptian and South African companies in the coming period.

articles.full_text:
Egypt and Zambia have begun follow-up talks aimed at expanding bilateral investment and trade cooperation following the Alamein–Africa Business Forum, with officials discussing joint projects, business-to-business meetings and opportunities under African trade agreements.
Egypt’s Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade hosted a roundtable with a Zambian delegation attended by Mohamed Awad, CEO of the General Authority for Investment and Free Zones, GAFI; Heba Salama, CEO of the COMESA Regional Investment Agency; Albert Halwampa, Director General of the Zambia Development Agency; and Zambia’s Ambassador to Egypt Toply Lubaya.
Representatives of the business communities of both countries also attended the meeting.
The discussions covered available investment opportunities, capital requirements and plans to arrange bilateral meetings between companies and government agencies in Egypt and Zambia.
Turning Alamein Forum Talks Into Investment
Awad said Egypt and Zambia should translate their longstanding relations into greater investment and trade flows capable of creating jobs and increasing local value added.
He also called for greater use of existing cooperation agreements between the two countries.
Awad presented recent changes to Egypt’s investment environment, including efforts to streamline procedures, expand digital services and make investment opportunities across the country more accessible to investors.
GAFI has been expanding digital services in 2026, including development of a new electronic portal designed to bring its investor services and platforms together in one system.
Salama said the roundtable represented a practical step toward implementing the outcomes of the Alamein–Africa Business Forum, which was held in New Alamein from October 2 to 4.
The forum, an Egyptian initiative endorsed by the African Union, was designed to expand intra-African trade, investment and private-sector partnerships and will be held every two years in Egypt.
Zambia Seeks More Egyptian Investment
Halwampa said Zambia was seeking deeper cooperation with Egypt through both COMESA and the African Continental Free Trade Area, AfCFTA.
He also expressed interest in drawing on GAFI’s experience in managing free and investment zones and preparing investment opportunities.
Zambia welcomes further Egyptian investment, particularly as Egyptian companies already operate in infrastructure and other sectors, he said.
The Zambian side also pointed to a recent visit by a delegation of Egyptian pharmaceutical companies as evidence of expanding commercial ties.
Healthcare has become one of the areas of growing cooperation. Egyptian and Zambian officials discussed pharmaceutical manufacturing and healthcare investment earlier this year, while Egypt delivered a 33-container pharmaceutical shipment to Zambia in June under an existing bilateral agreement.
The latest meeting builds on an investment cooperation memorandum signed between GAFI and the Zambia Development Agency in February 2025. The agreement covers the exchange of information on investment opportunities, regulations and policies, while encouraging companies in both countries to develop joint investment projects.
The new round of talks suggests Egypt and Zambia are now seeking to move beyond institutional agreements toward specific business partnerships and projects, particularly in infrastructure, healthcare, manufacturing and other sectors where both sides see opportunities for regional expansion.

articles.title: Africa's Business Leaders Are Ready to Trade With Each Other. The Systems Are Not ‎ - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: Africa's Business Leaders Are Ready to Trade With Each Other. The Systems Are Not ‎  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
African executives are betting on their own continent. Preliminary results from the 2026 PAFTRAC Africa CEO Trade Survey show that 81.3 per cent of senior business leaders expect their cross-border activity to grow over the next twelve months. Intra-African commerce has overtaken China, Europe and the United States as their main target destination.
The findings were presented at the WTO Public Forum in Geneva on 16 September, in a session convened by Afreximbank and the Pan-African Private Sector Trade and Investment Committee (PAFTRAC). The survey has grown from 400 respondents in 2021 to more than 2,500 this year, which makes it a significant gauge of executive sentiment.
Rising trade, flat share
Optimism is not yet showing up in the structure of African trade. According to the survey release, intra-African merchandise trade remains stuck at 15 to 18 per cent of total exports, despite the operational rollout of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Absolute numbers are moving, though slowly. Afreximbank's latest African Trade Report estimates intra-African trade at $213.8 billion in 2025, up 5.47 per cent from $202.7 billion in 2024.
Trade is growing, but not fast enough to change the continent's overall pattern. The same report projects that intra-African trade could double within a decade if the AfCFTA is fully implemented.
A tool many do not know about
The survey points to an information gap. While 70.2 per cent of respondents report a tangible operational impact from AfCFTA-related reforms, more than half are unfamiliar with the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS). Awareness of the E-Tariff Book, the African Trade Observatory and the AfCFTA's non-tariff barrier reporting tools is similarly limited.
This matters because PAPSS was built to address a core problem. Afreximbank and the AfCFTA Secretariat announced its operational roll-out in September 2021 as a continent-wide platform for clearing and settling intra-African payments.
Before PAPSS, over 80 per cent of cross-border payments from African banks had to be routed offshore for clearing. An instrument designed to cut that friction is unknown to much of the business community it was meant to serve.
The "prejudice premium"
The sharpest finding concerns the cost of money. According to IFC analysis cited by PAFTRAC, risk ratings from Western credit agencies impose an estimated excess premium of $31 billion a year on African sovereign and institutional borrowers.
Professor Patrick Utomi, PAFTRAC's Chairperson, calls this a "prejudice premium." He argues that when an economy actively at war can obtain more competitive financing than a stable, peaceful African sovereign, the system is misreading reality, and that outdated global rules and subjective rating methodologies act as a direct tax on African trade.
The squeeze reaches ordinary traders. Some 57 per cent of surveyed executives describe access to trade finance for cross-border transactions as difficult or very difficult. The IFC puts Africa's SME financing gap at more than $331 billion.
Afreximbank separately estimates a trade finance gap of about $100 billion a year, which it describes as a major constraint on the AfCFTA.These figures measure different things, but they point the same way.
What should change
The survey suggests Africa's trade challenge is no longer mainly a shortage of declarations or ambition. It is implementation, information and the cost of capital.
Three priorities follow:
Awareness: The AfCFTA Secretariat, central banks and trade bodies should take PAPSS and the digital trade tools directly to businesses, including small traders in border towns and markets.
SME finance: Trade finance must reach smaller firms, which carry the bulk of the financing gap.
Credit ratings: African institutions need a stronger voice in how sovereign risk is assessed and priced.
A note of caution
These are preliminary findings, and readers should weigh them accordingly. PAFTRAC is an advocacy platform, and its convening partner Afreximbank is also the developer of PAPSS, so the survey's emphasis on credit-rating bias and payment systems reflects institutional interests as well as data.
The IFC figures reach us only through PAFTRAC, and I could not locate the original IFC publication. The full report, due this month, should show how well the numbers hold up.
The core message still stands. African executives are ready to trade with one another, and most of the remaining barriers are ones African policymakers and institutions can choose to remove.

articles.title: African CEOs want more regional trade, but $31bn risk premium holds them back - Business News Nigeria
articles.summary: African CEOs want more regional trade, but $31bn risk premium holds them back  Business News Nigeria
articles.full_text:
African businesses are increasingly looking within the continent for growth, but expensive risk pricing, limited trade finance and weak implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) are preventing that ambition from translating into stronger intra-African commerce.
A new survey of more than 2,500 African business leaders found that 81.3 percent of senior executives expect their cross-border activity to increase over the next 12 months, signalling growing confidence in regional markets despite persistent structural barriers to trade.
The findings from the 2026 PAFTRAC Africa CEO Trade Survey show that intra-African commerce has now overtaken China, Europe and the United States as the principal target destination for surveyed executives.
Yet intra-African merchandise trade remains stuck at between 15 percent and 18 percent of Africa’s total exports, with little movement despite the operational rollout of AfCFTA.
The survey, conducted by the Pan-African Private Sector Trade and Investment Committee (PAFTRAC), points to a widening gap between what African businesses want to do and the financial and policy systems available to support them.
At the centre of that gap is the cost of capital. African sovereign and institutional borrowers face what the International Finance Corporation (IFC) estimates to be an excess financing premium of about $31 billion annually because of how African risk is priced by Western credit-rating agencies.
Patrick Utomi, chairperson of PAFTRAC, described the additional cost as a prejudice premium, arguing that global credit-rating methodologies can impose financing costs that do not adequately reflect the underlying economic and political conditions of African countries. “The core issue is risk perception,” Utomi said.
Read also: Finance firm targets importers with new office for cross-border payments
According to him, when stable African economies receive less competitive financing than countries facing severe instability, the resulting pricing structure effectively places an additional tax on African economies and their businesses.
For companies attempting to move goods across African borders, the consequences extend beyond government borrowing costs. The survey found that 57 percent of executives consider access to trade finance for cross-border transactions difficult or very difficult.
This means companies may have the market opportunity, customers and products needed to expand across borders, but still struggle to secure the working capital, guarantees, letters of credit and other financing required to execute transactions. The problem is particularly significant for small and medium-sized businesses, which dominate much of Africa’s private sector.
The IFC estimates Africa’s SME financing gap at more than $331 billion, leaving businesses with limited capacity to finance expansion at precisely the time when AfCFTA is supposed to make cross-border commerce easier.
The survey also exposes a second problem: the continent’s trade architecture is advancing faster than businesses’ understanding of how to use it.
While 70.2 percent of respondents said AfCFTA-related reforms have already had a tangible operational impact on their businesses, awareness of several of the agreement’s key implementation mechanisms remains low.
More than half of the executives surveyed are unfamiliar with the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), which was designed to enable African businesses to settle eligible cross-border transactions in African currencies and reduce dependence on dollar clearing.
Awareness is also limited around the E-Tariff Book, African Trade Observatory and AfCFTA’s mechanisms for reporting non-tariff barriers.
This creates a paradox for the continent’s largest trade integration project. African businesses increasingly want to trade across borders, and reforms are beginning to affect their operations, but many companies still lack knowledge of the systems intended to make that trade cheaper, faster and more predictable.
For businesses, the challenge is therefore no longer simply whether AfCFTA exists. It is whether the financial infrastructure, payment systems, customs processes, trade information and regulatory mechanisms surrounding it are accessible enough to make regional commerce commercially viable. The contrast is particularly striking when viewed against the survey’s expansion in scale.
PAFTRAC’s CEO Trade Survey has grown from 400 respondents in 2021 to more than 2,500 executives in 2026, making it one of the broadest measures of African private-sector sentiment on trade.
The latest findings show strong commercial appetite for regional integration, even as the continent’s trade statistics remain stubbornly weak. Intra-African merchandise exports have remained within the 15–18 percent range, far below the level of regional trade seen in more integrated markets.
This suggests that removing tariffs alone will not be enough to transform African trade. Businesses also need access to affordable financing, reliable payments, predictable regulations, functioning transport infrastructure and mechanisms that allow companies to resolve non-tariff barriers when they arise.
The financing issue is particularly important because higher perceived risk can raise costs throughout the trade chain. When banks and investors attach higher risk premiums to African transactions, businesses can face more expensive credit, larger collateral requirements and greater difficulty obtaining trade finance.
Those costs ultimately affect the price of goods and the ability of African companies to compete with international suppliers. For SMEs, the impact can be even greater because they typically have fewer financing options and weaker balance sheets than large corporations.
The result is that a company in one African country may identify a viable market in another African country but still decide against entering it because the cost and complexity of financing the transaction erodes the potential returns.
Read also: Nigeria’s trade with Africa is up 21%. What will it take for small businesses to share in it?
The findings put pressure on African policymakers to move the AfCFTA agenda beyond legal and institutional adoption towards practical execution.
The agreement has created the framework for a single African market, but businesses ultimately judge integration by whether they can move goods, receive payments, obtain financing and resolve regulatory problems at a lower cost.
The survey suggests that the private sector is already signalling where the demand lies. Four out of five executives expect their cross-border activity to increase over the next year, while intra-African markets have become their preferred destination for expansion.
The bigger question is whether African governments and financial institutions can reduce the barriers standing between that ambition and actual trade.
PAFTRAC’s preliminary findings were presented at the World Trade Organization Public Forum in Geneva. The full 2026 Africa CEO Trade Survey, scheduled for publication in October, is expected to provide further analysis of trade barriers, AfCFTA implementation and financing constraints, alongside policy recommendations from the more than 2,500 executives surveyed.

Alliance, a New York-headquartered crypto accelerator and founder community that invests in early-stage crypto and fintech startups, has invested $500,000 in equity in Cloud9, a Kenyan fintech that provides digital banking services for businesses.
The investment is part of Cloud9’s ongoing pre-seed round, which also attracted investment from Techstars NYC and strategic angel investors, bringing the company’s total funding to $1 million.
The investment comes as Cloud9 pushes beyond digital banking to build payment infrastructure for African businesses trading across borders after making two acquisitions in three months.
The company plans to use the new funding to expand its cross-border payment corridors, improve its product experience, launch virtual and physical cards, and grow its base of African consumers and businesses using the platform to participate in global trade.
Cloud9 launched its product in early 2026 and says it has since created more than 25,000 accounts, with transaction volume growing by more than 15% week over week. It is positioning the platform as financial infrastructure for African businesses trading across borders.
“Kenya already skipped the bank branch once. Mobile money became how the country pays for almost everything, but only within its borders,” said Tesh Mbaabu, Cloud9’s founder and chief executive officer. “With Cloud9, a merchant in Nairobi should be able to pay a supplier in Guangzhou as easily as they pay a vendor down the street. Where an entrepreneur is based should not limit who they can buy from or sell to.”
Cloud9 says users can hold multiple currencies, including Kenyan shillings, US dollars, euros, pounds and Chinese yuan. They can send payments to suppliers in more than 100 countries, receive international payments through virtual accounts, and withdraw funds to mobile money when they need local currency.
The company also offers tools for payroll, bulk payments and team approvals for businesses, while its Cloud9 Wealth product gives Kenyan users access to savings vaults and global stock markets. Its treasury operations cover more than 120 countries, and its payment network currently supports direct payments to Mainland China, Hong Kong, India and Southeast Asia, as well as intra-African collections and local-currency disbursements. The company said it is targeting businesses involved in global trade. Kenya imports from China were worth $4.31 billion in 2024.
Stablecoins are a key part of how Cloud9 moves money between countries. A customer may hold dollars, euros, or Kenyan shillings and initiate a payment in one of those currencies. Cloud9 then uses USDC or USDT to move value between countries and currencies on the backend.
“Stablecoins are becoming the settlement layer for global trade, and Africa is where that shift matters most,” said Imran Khan, general partner at Alliance. “Tesh has built for African merchants at scale before, and Cloud9 is turning stablecoin rails into an everyday bank account for the entrepreneurs who need it most.”

Tinubu assures manufacturers of Nigeria Industrial Policy implementation
President Bola Tinubu has assured manufacturers of the federal government’s commitment to the Nigeria Industrial Policy (NIP).
Mr Tinubu said the policy had a delivery mechanism to drive measurable improvements in the country’s industrial sector.
He gave the assurance at the sixth Adeola Odutola Lecture and 54th Annual General Meeting of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) on Tuesday in Lagos.
Mr Tinubu was represented by the Minister of State for Industry, John Enoh, at the event with the theme: “Leveraging National Industrial Policy to Position Nigeria as Africa’s Industrial Hub.”
The president said NIP implementation would be measured by factories reopening, increased capacity utilisation, jobs created, exports shipped and new factories established.
He also directed the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, through the Industrial Revolution Working Group (IRWG), to hold quarterly delivery dialogues with MAN to monitor implementation and hold the government accountable.
“That is why this policy is not a shelf document. It has a delivery engine. Implementation of the Nigerian industrial policy will be measured, reported, and published.
“For clarity, I have directed the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, through the IRWG, to hold a standing quarterly delivery dialogue with this association. This is so that you can hold us to account,” he said.
Mr Tinubu said the IRWG brought government, the organised private sector, financiers and development partners together under one scorecard.
He said the scorecard would measure factories reopening, capacity utilisation, jobs created, exports shipped and new factories established.
Mr Tinubu also identified energy, capital, markets, security and accountability as key areas requiring government intervention to accelerate industrialisation.
“We will continue to prioritise gas for industry and provide reliable power for industrial clusters because the cost of energy is the cost of everything we make,” he said.
The president said the government would work with the Bank of Industry, development finance institutions, and the banking system to provide patient, affordable, long-term financing to productive enterprises.
Mr Tinubu said the government’s Nigeria First policy would support public procurement of locally made goods that meet required standards.
He added that initiatives such as the National Single Window would reduce the cost and time of moving goods through ports and borders.
Mr Tinubu urged manufacturers to reciprocate the government’s efforts by investing in production capacity and deepening backward integration.
MAN president Francis Meshioye stressed the need for sustained improvements in productivity, investment, technology adoption, infrastructure, energy, finance and the broader business environment.
Mr Meshioye noted that although Nigeria’s total exports rose to N85.13 trillion in 2025, manufactured exports stood at only N2.50 trillion.
The MAN president urged the federal government to fast-track implementation of the NIP with clear timelines, measurable performance indicators and institutional accountability.
He also called for the establishment of a Nigeria First Industrial Fund to provide long-term concessionary financing and support technology upgrading.
“We also call for prioritisation of gas allocation to manufacturers, resolution of outstanding four per cent Free-on-Board levy and foreign exchange-forward obligations,” he said.
He also called for the elimination of duplicative regulatory inspections and improved coordination among regulatory agencies.
In his keynote address, Kandeh Yumkella, former director-general of the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation, said Nigeria had the essential foundations to become an industrial powerhouse.
He listed a large market, natural resources, entrepreneurial capacity, financial depth and strategic positioning within ECOWAS and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Mr Yumkella, however, said Nigeria’s industrial challenge was not a shortage of ambition or enterprise but converting the country’s scale into productivity, competitiveness and exports.
He identified reliable electricity as critical to Nigeria’s industrial transformation, noting that the country’s power grid currently delivers about 5,000 to 6,000 megawatts against an estimated demand of more than 20,000 megawatts.
According to him, manufacturers spent an estimated N1.34 trillion on self-generated power in 2025, up from N781.68 billion in 2023.
He said energy accounted for between 35 and 40 per cent of production costs.
Mr Yumkella called for greater investment in technical and vocational education and stronger industry-training partnerships to address the skills gap affecting manufacturers.
He said the AfCFTA had created a market of about 1.4 billion people with a combined GDP of about $3.4 trillion.
Mr Yumkella said this presented Nigeria with an opportunity to become a major production hub for the continent.
He urged the country to move beyond its position as Africa’s largest consumer market to becoming one of its leading production centres.

articles.title: From Seoul To Jakarta: How Sisi’s Asia Tour Could Boost Egypt’s Economy - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: From Seoul To Jakarta: How Sisi’s Asia Tour Could Boost Egypt’s Economy  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi’s tour of South Korea, Malaysia and Indonesia marks a wider attempt by Cairo to deepen its economic links with Asia, attract export-oriented manufacturing and build political partnerships extending from Northeast Asia to Southeast Asia.
El-Sisi arrived in Seoul on October 6 for the first leg of the tour. He is scheduled to hold a summit with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and meet executives from major Korean companies before travelling to Malaysia and Indonesia. The Egyptian Presidency has described the trip as part of efforts to expand political, economic and investment cooperation with Asian economies.
South Korea’s presidential office said the summit agenda would include trade, investment, infrastructure, supply chains, people-to-people ties and international affairs. The visit is El-Sisi’s first to South Korea since 2016.
Seoul: From Korean Investment To Industrial Localization
South Korea is the most industrially focused stop.
When Lee visited Cairo in November 2025, Egypt identified automobiles, shipbuilding, artificial intelligence, telecommunications, petrochemicals and mining as priority sectors and invited Korean companies to manufacture in Egypt rather than simply export to it. Cairo also proposed greater Korean industrial activity inside the Suez Canal Economic Zone.
That agenda has since moved toward a possible Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. Egypt and South Korea signed a joint statement in January 2026 launching the next stage toward CEPA negotiations after a joint feasibility study. The proposed framework would cover investment, technology transfer, industrial development and trade liberalization.
Existing Korean manufacturers provide a base for expansion. Egyptian government data say Korean companies operating in Egypt produce goods worth more than $1.5 billion annually, around 80% of which are exported to 47 countries, while providing more than 6,000 direct jobs. Samsung and Hyundai Rotem are among the major investors.
The Seoul meetings will therefore be watched for movement from general investment commitments toward new factories, supply-chain agreements and progress on CEPA.
Malaysia: ASEAN Access And A First Presidential Visit
Malaysia represents a different opportunity. This is El-Sisi’s first visit to the country since becoming president in 2014, and Malaysian officials expect him in Kuala Lumpur later this week.
Egypt and Malaysia agreed in 2024 to work toward a strategic partnership and identified the digital economy, agricultural commodities, renewable-energy infrastructure, maritime transport, manufacturing and semiconductors as areas for expansion.
Bilateral trade reached about $718 million in 2025, according to Egyptian government data. Cooperation has also moved into manufacturing through local assembly of Malaysia’s Proton Saga cars in Egypt.
The broader economic logic is geographical: Egyptian manufacturers can use Egypt’s trade agreements to reach African, Arab and European-linked markets, while stronger Malaysian ties can give Egyptian businesses greater access to ASEAN economies.
Jakarta: Turning Strategic Partnership Into Projects
Indonesia is the tour’s most politically developed Southeast Asian relationship.
El-Sisi and President Prabowo Subianto signed a declaration establishing an Egypt-Indonesia strategic partnership in April 2025, covering manufacturing, investment, ICT, food security and energy.
Trade between the countries reached around $1.7 billion in 2024, with Indonesia running a substantial surplus. Egyptian exports totaled about $151 million, while imports from Indonesia reached roughly $1.6 billion.
Both governments have identified palm oil, fertilizers, renewable energy, agriculture, infrastructure, transport and the digital economy as possible growth sectors. They have also discussed using Egypt as a platform for Indonesian access to African and Euro-Mediterranean markets and Indonesia as a gateway for Egyptian products into ASEAN.
More Than An Investment Tour
The political dimension is equally important.
Egypt, Malaysia and Indonesia share positions supporting Palestinian statehood and opposing the displacement of Palestinians, while Cairo and Jakarta have also coordinated on freedom of navigation and regional stability.
For Egypt, the significance of the tour will ultimately depend on what follows the presidential meetings: signed investments, factories, trade agreements and financing commitments.
The trip therefore represents less a ceremonial swing through Asia than an attempt to connect Egypt’s manufacturing, logistics and export ambitions with three of Asia’s most important industrial and emerging-market partners.

articles.title: Why Nigeria is missing from Airtel Money’s $7bn IPO - TechCabal
articles.summary: Why Nigeria is missing from Airtel Money’s $7bn IPO  TechCabal
articles.full_text:
When Airtel Money lists on the London Stock Exchange later this month, it will do so without its struggling Nigerian fintech business. A Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) directive required the mobile money business to transfer its 25% stake in SmartCash, the vehicle through which Airtel operates its Nigerian fintech business, back to Airtel Networks Limited, its Nigerian telecom subsidiary, according to Airtel Money’s IPO prospectus.
The deal was completed for $3 million. But Airtel Money says it is exploring ways to bring SmartCash back into the group. However, the Nigerian business will not be part of the fintech company investors are buying when it lists on October 14.
“The Group is exploring options to bring Smartcash Nigeria within the Group’s perimeter, consistent with the structure of the Group’s other operations,” Airtel Money said in its IPO prospectus. “There can be no assurance as to the timing or outcome of these, which remain subject to regulatory approvals.”
The prospectus describes the group as a pan-African fintech platform operating in 13 African countries and serving approximately 53 million monthly active users as of June 30, 2026.
Airtel’s situation in Nigeria is part of a broader shift among Africa’s telecom companies increasingly trying to separate their fintech businesses from their core telecom operations. They see mobile money as a business that needs its own capital structures, management focus, growth strategies, and is valued separately from the telecom networks that helped create it.
In April, MTN Nigeria shareholders approved the separation of MoMo Payment Service Bank and Y’ello Digital Financial Services from MTN Nigeria into a new holding structure backed by MTN Group, subject to regulatory approval. MTN Group completed the separation of its mobile money business in Ghana in April.
The Nigerian PSB problem
Since the CBN introduced Payment Service Banks (PSBs) in 2018, telecom-led fintechs have struggled to turn their subscriber scale into financial services dominance because of licence restrictions and their late entry into an already developing market.
PSBs can accept deposits and facilitate payments, but lending is restricted, removing one of the most lucrative ways fintech companies monetise customers.
At the same time, companies such as OPay and PalmPay entered the market with products built around payments, credit and merchant services, and have built large distribution networks of their own.
Large telecom operators have struggled to turn their distribution advantage into fintech scale. MTN and Airtel have a combined 167.62 million subscribers, representing 86.02% of Nigeria’s telecom market, but their mobile money businesses have yet to reach 10 million subscribers combined. OPay, meanwhile, had 39.3 million monthly active users in 2025.
Nigeria’s mobile money market processed ₦20.71 trillion ($13.49 billion) in Q1 2025. By year-end, OPay alone reported a gross transaction value of $358 billion.
In 2025, MTN Nigeria chief executive officer Karl Toriola said the company initially expected MoMo PSB to reach about 20 million monthly active users, but revised those expectations because of competition from OPay and PalmPay, the maturity of cash-in and cash-out networks, and the limitations of the PSB licence.
“The MoMo PSB licence does have its limitations, and we need to look at add-ons to that licence to really evolve in that market to get to where we are,” Toriola said. “So, without a doubt, we are behind our initial excitement about the MoMo PSB, but we are well grounded in reality.”
Airtel has also acknowledged the competitiveness of the Nigerian market. “In Nigeria, it is a well-developed fintech market, compared to many other markets,” Sunil Taldar, Airtel Africa’s CEO, said in 2025.
Both operators are still doubling down on their mobile money businesses. SmartCash is pushing a zero-fee banking model and a 15% annual interest rate on savings deposits. It has also integrated with multiple banks and financial institutions, allowing wallet transfers and interbank transactions across its network as it tries to capture more of the transfer market.
MTN, meanwhile, is investing in more agents and merchants, deeper rural penetration, and expanding its digital payments capacity as it tries to increase transaction volumes.
Smartcash could still return
Airtel Money is about to become one of Africa’s biggest publicly listed fintech businesses. It has priced its London initial public offering at £1.96 ($2.59) per share, valuing the mobile money business at £5.3 billion ($7 billion) ahead of its October 14 debut.
Nigeria is Airtel Africa’s second-largest telecom region by subscribers and one of Africa’s biggest fintech markets. Yet it accounted for only 1.24% of Airtel mobile money’s $404 million quarterly revenue and 6.02% of its customer base as of June 2026.
That makes the Nigerian business a small part of the group being taken public, but a noticeable absence given the potential size of the Nigerian market.
Airtel’s fintech operations in Nigeria are currently conducted through Airtel Networks Limited, reflecting the CBN’s licencing requirements, under which mobile money and payment service bank licences must be held by an entity with the relevant telco licence and local regulatory oversight.
Airtel Networks holds the majority shareholding in SmartCash Nigeria, while a nominee shareholding within the group’s perimeter currently stands at below 0.01%.
“Notwithstanding that it sits outside the Group’s perimeter, the Group’s management team provides limited guidance and support to SmartCash Nigeria in respect of technical expertise and management services, reflecting the Group’s integrated approach to fintech operations across its African footprint,” Airtel Money said of its continued support for SmartCash in its prospectus.
The company said the support is not considered material to the group’s current operations, strategy or resource allocation.
For now, SmartCash remains outside Airtel Money’s group, even as the company explores ways to bring it back. Whether that changes Airtel’s fortunes in Nigeria will depend less on where SmartCash sits and more on whether it can turn its telecom scale into a fintech business capable of competing with the likes of OPay and PalmPay.
