Egypt’s cabinet said on Tuesday that the Egypt Forum 2026 will feature sessions on foreign-currency resources, debt management and implementation of the National Economic Transformation Program over the coming years.
The forum, which will run from 19 to 24 October, will also address other priorities for the next phase, issues of public concern and government decisions, plans and programs aimed at improving living conditions.
This was announced during a meeting as part of ongoing preparations for the event, slated for 19 to 24 October.
The two sessions, titled “Outlines of the Egyptian Economic Programme through 2030” and “Foreign Currency Resources and Debt Management”, will bring together economists and specialists to discuss the issues in depth and address concerns raised by the public and in the media, according to a cabinet statement.
One session will officially present the National Economic Transformation Program, according to a cabinet statement.
The program was designed to guide Egypt's economic priorities in the next phase, boost the economy’s competitiveness, and ensure sustainable public debt management.
It also aims to improve coordination between fiscal and monetary policy after the country’s $8 billion economic reform program with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) concludes in December 2026.
The IMF program was approved in 2024 after an expansion of a previous $3 billion facility to help Egypt deal with a foreign-currency shortage, high inflation and external financing needs.
The fund highlighted that Egypt’s continued focus on boosting foreign capital, fiscal consolidation, debt management, and state-asset sales can reduce its high external financing needs.
During the meeting, Madbouly confirmed the government’s intent to continue prioritizing public debt management, while sustaining the downward trajectory of external debt for the medium and long-term.
He also asserted the government’s commitment to attract more direct investment flows across several sectors, which will, in turn, help to secure alternative sources of funding.
At the end of the first quarter of 2026, Egypt’s external debt rose to $164.8 billion, up from $161.2 billion at the end of June 2025, while its ratio to GDP fell to 38.9 percent from 44.2 percent.
Furthermore, the government is also planning to reduce this debt by a further $1.5–2 billion annually to ease external repayment obligations, as they account for 26.3 percent, or $43.1 billion, of the country’s total obligations, owed mainly to institutions, such as the IMF.
This aligns with the state’s plan to reduce the budget-sector debt to around 78 percent of the GDP this FY 2026/2027, from 81.8 percent the previous fiscal year.
The second session will examine the role of monetary policy in supporting economic stability through coordination between the government and the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE), as well as measures to encourage private-sector participation and increase and diversify foreign-currency inflows.
Egypt’s net international reserves rose by 1.6 percent or $920 million in August to a new record $57.2 billion, up from $56.29 billion at the end of July.
This rise was driven by a sharp increase in the value of the CBE’s gold reserves, policy reforms, increased Suez Canal and tourism revenues, and rising remittance inflows, all of which are major sources of foreign currency.
Reserves have maintained a high level since the CBE implemented a six-percentage-point interest rate hike in March 2024 to curb high inflation, stabilize prices in the domestic market, and boost foreign currency liquidity and manage pressure on the country’s currency.
The state has also been working to create opportunities to utilize the private sector as the main driver of development to create sustainable job opportunities, increase value-added output, and deepen local manufacturing.
This will, in turn, improve Egypt’s macroeconomic stability, increase its ability to withstand shocks amid geopolitical tensions, and expand the private sector’s contribution to the economy to more than 65 percent by 2030.

The Democratic Republic of Congo has rolled out a countrywide airborne geological mapping initiative designed to sharpen understanding of its mineral wealth, lower exploration risk and pull investment into areas that have seen little scrutiny, its geological agency said.
Congo holds the title of the planet's biggest cobalt producer and ranks first in Africa for copper output, yet officials estimate that fewer than one-tenth of the nation's land area has been properly surveyed. The government has been consolidating its hold on the mining industry, chasing a bigger slice of income from current operations while bringing geological data that shapes future finds under state control.
Operating under the name PC2G-RDC, the effort will employ high-resolution airborne geophysical surveys to deepen geological understanding of Congo's subsurface, assisting in the location of mineral-rich zones and widening scientific knowledge of underground resources, the National Geological Service of the Congo (SGNC) said in a Monday statement.
SGNC is carrying out the programme alongside Spanish geophysics company Xcalibur, which provides technical assistance. According to the statement, attention will centre on Kongo Central, Kwango, Kwilu and Greater Kasai, extending earlier work completed in Greater Katanga.
Speaking at the launch, Mines Minister Louis Watum Kabamba said the initiative would raise the nation's geoscientific coverage from 22.27% to 46.1%.
SGNC Director General Raoul Wazenga Vitima remarked that sovereignty does not start at the moment a mineral is pulled from the ground, but rather when the state is familiar with its territory, holds its own maps, governs its data, keeps its samples, builds its laboratories and cultivates specialists who can read that information. He added that Congo ought not merely to be better mapped, but should progressively gain the ability to map itself.
Officials indicated the surveys would update existing datasets, assist in uncovering fresh prospective zones and bolster the state's ability to plan and negotiate resource development.

articles.title: Zambia to secure $1.5 billion US health support after data-sharing differences are resolved - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Zambia to secure $1.5 billion US health support after data-sharing differences are resolved  Business Insider AfricaZambia to sign deal for $1.5 bn in US health funding  ECR
articles.full_text:
- Zambia will sign a $1.5 billion, five-year health funding agreement with the United States after resolving disputes over data sharing.
- The new pact targets HIV/AIDS, malaria, maternal and child health, and boosts Zambia’s disease outbreak preparedness.
- Zambia paused negotiations earlier this year over U.S. demands for broad access to health data and concerns of possible links to Zambia’s mineral resources.
- The final deal limits U.S. data access strictly to program monitoring and removes a clause about sharing patient medical specimens.
Zambia is set to sign a new health funding agreement with the United States worth $1.5 billion over five years after resolving concerns over Washington’s demands for access to medical data, the country’s health minister said.
The agreement will support HIV/AIDS and malaria programmes, maternal and child health services and efforts to strengthen Zambia’s preparedness for disease outbreaks. Under the pact, the US will provide $1.5 billion, while Zambia will contribute $2.1 billion towards health programmes over the five years.
Data-sharing concerns delayed the deal
Zambia had previously paused negotiations over the agreement in February after raising concerns about data privacy and provisions that appeared to require broader access to health information. The government also faced questions over whether the proposed US health support was connected to negotiations around Zambia’s critical mineral resources.
Zambia is one of Africa’s major copper producers and has become increasingly important to global efforts to secure supplies of critical minerals needed for industries including energy and technology.
Health Minister Elijah Muchima said the final agreement would limit data-sharing to information needed to monitor and evaluate programmes funded by the US, Reuters reported. A provision requiring Zambia to provide patient medical specimens to the US upon request has also been removed.
The minister said there was no reference to critical minerals in the health agreement and that he was not aware of a separate critical minerals agreement being negotiated with Washington.
The US remains a major funder of health programmes in Zambia, particularly those focused on HIV/AIDS, malaria and public health.
The agreement follows similar health pacts signed between the US and other African countries, including Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, under a broader shift in Washington’s foreign aid policy towards helping recipient countries become more self-reliant.

Dubai’s DP World has secured a 10-year extension until 2051 for its concession to operate a multipurpose terminal in Angola and committed new investments to expand the port of Luanda, the African country’s capital.
The global ports operator has invested more than $260 million to upgrade and modernise the terminal since operations there began in 2021.
Over the past five years cargo volume handled at the terminal has nearly doubled to more than 350,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), supported by an additional 28,000 square metres of yard area, the company said in a statement.
DP World will invest a further $90 million over the next two years to expand and enhance the terminal’s infrastructure, equipment and operational capabilities.
The expansion will extend the quay by 222 metres, the operating area by 100,000 square metres and the terminal’s design capacity to 1.2 million TEUs.
Mohammed Akoojee, CEO for Africa at DP World, said the ability to handle larger vessels would support new shipping services and strengthen the terminal’s potential as a gateway for West and Central Africa.

articles.full_text:
In Nigeria, “please send your account details” has become almost as ordinary as exchanging phone numbers.
NIBSS recorded over 11 billion electronic payment transactions in 2024, with their value exceeding ₦1.07 quadrillion.
That growth has changed the demands placed on the institutions moving money around the country and across West Africa.
For banks, payment infrastructure is no longer something customers think about only when a transaction fails; it determines how quickly and reliably they can pay, receive and do business.
In this interview, Techeconomy speaks with Chinwe Uzoho, regional managing director for West Africa at Network International, about the state of payments infrastructure in the region, how banks are approaching modernisation, and what the next chapter of digital payments could mean for financial institutions and their customers.
Techeconomy (TE): West Africa is seeing a rapid transition toward digital payments, with mobile money accounts in sub-Saharan Africa surpassing 1.1 billion in 2025. From your vantage point at Network International, how would you describe the current state of payments infrastructure across the region, and how are banks modernising their infrastructure to meet this growing digital demand?
Chinwe Uzoho (CU): West Africa's payments landscape has evolved significantly over the last few years. What we are witnessing today is not simply a shift from cash to digital, but a complete transformation in how consumers and businesses interact with financial services.
In Nigeria specifically, digital payments have become part of everyday life, driven by growing smartphone penetration, fintech innovation, real-time payment rails, and increasing customer expectations for seamless experiences.
Banks are responding by moving away from monolithic, legacy infrastructures and investing in cloud-enabled platforms, API-driven ecosystems, data analytics capabilities, and real-time processing engines.
What is particularly encouraging is that modernisation is no longer viewed as a technology project. It is now a business growth strategy. Banks recognise that delivering faster onboarding, frictionless payments, and personalised customer experiences directly impacts customer acquisition and retention.
At Network International, we process billions of transactions annually for banks, fintechs, governments and merchants across the Middle East and Africa, operating in more than 50 countries and trusted by over 240,000 merchants and 250+ banks, fintechs and telcos.
Against this backdrop, we are seeing financial institutions increasingly prioritise scalable payment infrastructure that enables them to innovate faster while maintaining resilience, security, and regulatory compliance.
The institutions leading this transformation are those building agile ecosystems that can easily integrate with fintechs, merchants, and emerging digital channels.
Modern payment infrastructure is also enabling SMEs to access digital commerce, working capital, embedded finance and cross-border trade opportunities that were previously unavailable, broadening the impact of this transformation well beyond the banking sector.
TE: Digital transaction values in Nigeria alone surged past ₦1.07 quadrillion in 2024, according to the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System. What is driving this surge, and how are banks adapting their payments infrastructure to support this growth?
CU: The ₦1.07 quadrillion milestone demonstrates the remarkable pace of digital payments adoption in Nigeria and highlights the country's position as one of Africa's most dynamic fintech markets.
Transaction values on NIBSS platforms increased from approximately ₦600 trillion in 2023 to over ₦1.07 quadrillion in 2024, while transaction volumes exceeded 11 billion transactions.
Several factors are driving this growth:
First, consumers and businesses increasingly prefer digital channels because of their convenience and speed.
Second, Nigeria's thriving fintech ecosystem has expanded access to digital financial services across multiple customer segments.
Third, ongoing cashless initiatives and improved payment rails have accelerated behavioural change.
To support this growth, banks are investing in infrastructure capable of handling high transaction volumes in real time.
This includes upgrading switching platforms, strengthening API architectures, enhancing processing capacity, and improving system redundancy to ensure continuous availability.
The focus today is not simply supporting higher volumes; it is ensuring payments are completed instantly, securely, and reliably regardless of transaction peaks. 
TE: Legacy systems are one of the limitations many banks face. With over 60% of African banks still running on older core banking infrastructure, what does modernisation look like in 2026, is it full system replacement or incremental upgrades?
CU: In my view, modernisation in 2026 is less about replacing everything overnight and more about adopting a pragmatic transformation approach.
Many banks cannot afford the disruption associated with a complete core replacement. Instead, we are seeing successful institutions progressively modernise specific layers of their technology stacks while continuing to operate critical legacy systems.
This typically involves introducing API layers, migrating selected workloads to cloud environments, deploying modern payment hubs, and digitising customer-facing channels first.
These improvements allow banks to deliver innovation quickly while reducing operational risk. The most successful modernisation strategies are business-led rather than technology-led.
Banks are asking: "What capabilities do our customers need?" and "How can technology help us deliver them faster?" The answers increasingly revolve around agility, interoperability, and scalability rather than wholesale replacement.
TE: Banks and fintechs are collaborating more in recent times, especially as fintech investment in Africa crossed $2 billion in recent years. From your experience, what models of bank–fintech partnerships are actually working in West Africa to modernise payments infrastructure, and which are failing?
CU: The most successful partnerships are those where both parties contribute complementary strengths.
Banks bring regulatory expertise, trust, liquidity, and large customer bases. Fintechs bring innovation, agility, customer-centric product design, and speed to market.
The partnership models delivering the strongest impact include Banking-as-a-Service arrangements, API-based integrations, merchant acquiring partnerships, embedded finance solutions, and digital lending ecosystems.
In Nigeria, some of the strongest results have emerged when banks focus on what they do best and allow fintech partners to accelerate innovation around customer experiences.
Where partnerships tend to struggle is when objectives are unclear or when one party views the other as a competitor rather than a collaborator. Successful partnerships require shared incentives, clear governance frameworks, and a common understanding of customer value.
TE: Financial inclusion is still uneven. Despite progress made, about 45% of adults in sub-Saharan Africa are still unbanked. What specific infrastructure gaps continue to limit access, particularly in rural and underserved communities, and how can banks address them through payments infrastructure modernisation?
CU: While progress has been significant, financial inclusion remains an important opportunity across the region.
According to figures cited by the Central Bank of Nigeria, financial inclusion reached approximately 74% in 2023, up from 68% in 2020. However, millions of adults remain underserved, particularly in rural communities.
Infrastructure challenges remain a key barrier. These include limited broadband connectivity, inconsistent power availability, low digital literacy, insufficient agent networks in remote areas, and limited access to affordable digital devices.
Addressing these challenges requires collaboration across the public and private sectors.
The future of inclusion will not be driven solely by traditional bank branches. It will be enabled through mobile-first services, agent banking networks, interoperable payment ecosystems, and digital identity frameworks that make onboarding simpler and more accessible.
The goal should be to ensure financial services are available wherever people live, work, and transact.

Nigeria's NIBSS Instant Payments platform now processes billions of transactions annually and has become a critical component of the country's digital economy.
To support this demand, banks are investing in high-availability architectures, cloud-enabled infrastructure, automated monitoring tools, and real-time transaction processing capabilities.

Over the past month, Tanzania has advanced investment and trade discussions with Qatar, Oman, Vietnam, Russia and Burundi, while also taking its investment case to European markets. Together, the engagements are part of a government drive to build a broader network of commercial relationships across the Gulf, Asia, Africa and Europe.
This diplomatic tour culminates in the Tanzania Investment Forum in London on 8 October. Convened by the Tanzanian High Commission and Invest Africa, the forum will bring Prime Minister Mwigulu Nchemba and a government delegation together with investors, development finance institutions and business leaders to showcase investment opportunities across the country.
Tanzania has pursued a deliberate strategy of diversifying its partnerships and sources of investment, with the Gulf being a particular focus for Tanzania in recent years. Tanzania and Qatar signed a double-taxation agreement on 29 September, reflecting both countries’ growing cross-border business and willingness to facilitate future business opportunities. With an Omani delegation visiting Dar es Salaam at the same time, Tanzania has been described as an important East African partner, with a deep shared history and untapped opportunity in trade and logistics on the Indian Ocean Rim.
To the east, the second Vietnam–Tanzania Joint Commission sought to turn longstanding ties into projects. Officials advanced work on investment protection and double-taxation agreements, while companies pursued opportunities in agriculture, agro-processing, mining and the marine economy. Bilateral trade has grown, with Vietnam describing Tanzania as a bridge into East Africa. Tanzania, in turn, has presented the relationship as an effective entry point into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) markets, helping to develop stable supply chains for cashew nuts, cotton, timber and minerals.
In Europe, a Tanzanian delegation visited the EU’s only nickel smelter before heading to Italy to discuss investment opportunities in coffee processing and power transmission. With substantial nickel reserves and growing demand for critical minerals, Tanzania is using these engagements to attract investment across the value chain, positioning the country as an alternative, reliable trading partner.
This is where Tanzania’s geography matters. Its Indian Ocean coastline and links into East and Central Africa give it the potential to serve as a trading and logistics hub connecting African markets with the Gulf and Asia. Its engagements with Vietnam and Oman also reflect a practical form of South–South cooperation. This cooperation is supported by government coordination and shared commercial interests that open routes between emerging markets.
London has a stake in that development. As a global centre for finance, trade and commodities, it can provide capital, expertise and existing commercial networks for projects linking Tanzania’s resources and products to regional and international markets.
There is an opportunity to convert Tanzania’s growing network of ties into partnerships and investment. The Tanzania Investment Forum’s broad showcase of opportunities across energy, mining, infrastructure, logistics, agribusiness, manufacturing, technology, finance and tourism will provide a platform to turn recent diplomatic engagement into lasting commercial partnerships.

articles.title: From Chivayo to Wigwe: High-profile Africans killed in helicopter crashes - The Africa Report
articles.summary: From Chivayo to Wigwe: High-profile Africans killed in helicopter crashes  The Africa ReportWicknell Chivayo dead: President Emmerson Mnangagwa mourn Zimbabwe businessman wey die wit im wife for helicopter crash  BBCThe huge payout Chivayo’s first wife won, and the billions she was still fighting for  Daily NationMALAIKA MAHLATSI | Are the people celebrating Chivayo’s death immoral or is it the system that created him?  EWNWicknell Chivayo’s gifts: The pri...
articles.full_text:
The helicopter crash that killed Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo has put the spotlight back on a grim trail of air accidents that have claimed some of Africa’s most prominent figures over the past two years.
Chivayo, one of Zimbabwe’s most politically connected businessmen who served an effective three-year prison sentence after a 2005 money-laundering conviction, died alongside his wife, Lucy Muteke, and three others when their helicopter crashed at Kudenga Farm in Marondera, east of Harare, on 30 September.
Investigators are still trying to establish what brought the aircraft down.
Chivayo, 43, became known for his conspicuous displays of wealth, philanthropy and access to political leaders. His company, Intratrek Zimbabwe, won major state energy contracts, while his social-media feeds were filled with luxury cars, cash giveaways and encounters with African leaders, including Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa and Kenya’s William Ruto.
But Chivayo is only the latest big name on a striking list.
Herbert Wigwe, Abimbola Ogunbanjo and the US crash
On 9 February 2024, a helicopter crash in California’s Mojave Desert stunned Nigeria’s business establishment.
Herbert Wigwe, the banking titan and group CEO of Access Holdings, was flying to Las Vegas, where a Super Bowl LVIII was being held two days later, when the Airbus EC130 carrying him crashed near Halloran Springs.
Also aboard were his wife Doreen, their son Chizi, and Abimbola Ogunbanjo, former chairman of the Nigerian Exchange Group. All four passengers and the two pilots were killed.
Wigwe was one of Nigeria’s best-known bankers, having helped transform Access Bank from a relatively small lender into one of Africa’s largest financial institutions. Ogunbanjo, a prominent corporate lawyer, was the first group chairman of NGX Group after previously heading the National Council of the Nigerian Stock Exchange.
The subsequent US investigation blamed the accident on the pilot’s decision to continue under visual flight rules as weather conditions worsened. Investigators found that he became disoriented and lost control of the helicopter.
The crash that killed Kenya’s military chief
Two months later, Kenya lost its highest-ranking military officer.
General Francis Ogolla, Chief of the Kenya Defence Forces, was killed on 18 April 2024 when the Bell UH-1H-II military helicopter carrying him crashed shortly after take-off near Cheptulel in West Pokot County.
Ogolla was visiting troops deployed under Operation Maliza Uhalifu, the government’s campaign against banditry in the North Rift.
Nine other military personnel were killed, including Brigadier Swale Saidi, Colonel Duncan Keittany, Lieutenant Colonel David Sawe, Major George Benson Magondu, Captain Sora Mohamed, Captain Hillary Litali, Senior Sergeant John Kinyua Mureithi, Sergeant Cliphonce Omondi and Sergeant Rose Nyawira. Two others survived.
A fighter pilot who joined the military in 1984, Ogolla rose through the ranks to command the Kenya Air Force before President William Ruto appointed him defence chief in April 2023. He died just 10 days short of a year in the job.
The military investigation blamed the crash on an engine malfunction that cut power to the helicopter soon after it took off.
Ghana loses two ministers in one flight
On 6 August 2025, Ghana suffered the heaviest political loss among the crashes on this list. A Ghana Armed Forces Z-9 helicopter carrying an official delegation to Obuasi crashed in the Ashanti Region, killing all eight people aboard.
Among them were Defence Minister Edward Omane Boamah and Environment Minister Ibrahim Murtala Muhammed (pictured below). Boamah, a medical doctor and veteran of President John Mahama’s governments, had previously served as communications minister.
Muhammed, the MP for Tamale Central, had held several government positions before being appointed environment minister in 2025.
The crash also killed other senior figures in Mahama’s political and security establishment: Alhaji Muniru Mohammed Limuna, acting deputy national security coordinator, and Samuel Sarpong, vice-chairman of the governing National Democratic Congress and a former Central Regional Minister. Former parliamentary candidate Samuel Aboagye was also killed.
The three military crew were Squadron Leader Peter Bafemi Anala, Flying Officer Manin Twum-Ampadu and Sergeant Ernest Addo Mensah.
Investigators later blamed the crash on a downdraft as the helicopter flew over high ground in worsening weather, causing it to lose altitude and lift.
Kenyan MP Johana Ng’eno’s final flight
Kenya was struck again on 28 February 2026 when Johana Ng’eno, the MP for Emurua Dikirr, was killed in a helicopter crash in Nandi County.
Ng’eno had represented the constituency since 2013 and was serving his third consecutive term in parliament.
He died alongside retired Lt Col George Were, who was flying the helicopter; his aide and photographer Nicholas Kiplangat Koskei; aides Robert Kipkoech Keter and Wycliffe Kiprotich Rono; and Kenya Forest Service officer Amos Kipnetich Rotich.
Beyond the big names: the military toll
The headline deaths tell only part of the story. Helicopter crashes have also killed military personnel deployed on combat, peacekeeping and surveillance missions across the continent.
Uganda: Pilots killed en route to the Congo war
On 2 January 2024, a UPDF combat helicopter heading towards Democratic Republic of Congo crashed into a house in Uganda’s Ntoroko area. The two pilots, Lt Allan Tukamuhabwa Kapando and Lt Swadiq Aroma, were killed, as was John Mukidi, the civilian whose house was struck.
The helicopter was heading towards DRC in connection with Operation Shujaa, Uganda’s joint campaign with Congolese forces against the Allied Democratic Forces. The UPDF attributed the crash to bad weather.
Somalia: Five Ugandan soldiers killed
On 2 July 2025, five Ugandan military personnel were killed when a UPDF Mi-24 serving with the African Union mission in Somalia crashed at Mogadishu’s Aden Adde International Airport.
The helicopter was on its way back from escorting troops when it went down shortly before landing. Ammunition carried on board exploded after the crash.
Five personnel were killed. The three survivors — the pilot, co-pilot and flight engineer — suffered serious burns.
DRC: Three foreign aircrew die in Kinshasa
On 30 October 2024, a Congolese military helicopter crashed while attempting to land at N’Dolo airport in Kinshasa, killing its pilot, co-pilot and technician.
All three were foreign nationals working with the Congolese military, although authorities did not publicly identify them or disclose their nationalities.
Equatorial Guinea: Four airmen vanish in the forest
In June 2026, an Equatorial Guinean military Z-9 disappeared during a mission over the country’s continental region.
Weeks of searching eventually located the wreckage in difficult forested terrain between Niefang and Evinayong. All four crew members were dead.
Authorities recovered the aircraft’s black box as they sought to establish what caused the crash.

articles.title: Russia downplays plague reports as Trump offers US help - eNCA
articles.summary: Russia downplays plague reports as Trump offers US help  eNCARussian plague scare — what we know so far  CNNThe plague may have escaped from a lab in Siberia  The EconomistTrump says US will help Russia after plague death in Siberia  MoneywebWhat is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?  BBC
articles.full_text:
MOSCOW - Russia sought to downplay reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague, even as President Donald Trump said Washington was closely monitoring the situation and offered US help.
Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.
"We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.
"We'll help them, we'll help them as much as we can."
The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.
As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating.
But Russian officials stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease.
Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".
He said on Telegram that Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had determined, following tests, that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".
He added that there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the woman's death.
Kobzev said the sanitary-epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was "stable".
"The situation remains under our control and that of the experts."
Asked about the situation on Monday, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements rather than... rumours and speculations".
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.
- AFP

articles.title: Military plane crash kills 32 in Nigeria - eNCA
articles.summary: Military plane crash kills 32 in Nigeria  eNCANigerian military helicopter with 32 passengers, crew crashes  SABC NewsNigeria's Tinubu confirms 32 dead after military plane crash  EWNNigeria mourns 32 killed as military plane crashes into swamp  CLUB OF MOZAMBIQUENigerian Air Force plane crash: Bola Tinubu declares three days of mourning as 25 killed  BBC
articles.full_text:
LAGOS - A Nigerian Air Force plane crashed on Monday in the country's southwest, killing all 32 people on board, President Bola Tinubu said, declaring three days of national mourning.
It is one of the worst air disasters in recent years in Africa's most populous country.
The passenger aircraft was on a "routine mission" from Benin City in southern Nigeria to the economic hub of Lagos when it went down at Igbokoda in southwestern Ondo state shortly after 9am, the president and the air force said.
"The president extends his deepest condolences to the family of the 25 passengers and seven crew members involved," Tinubu's office said in a statement.
"This is a painful moment for our armed forces and for the entire nation," he said.
Tinubu's spokesman Bayo Onanuga said in a later statement that the president "has declared a three-day national mourning for Air Force personnel who died in the crash".
He also directed that flags be flown at half-staff across the country to pay respect to the officers.
The Air Force will release the identities of the victims after notifying their families, the presidency said.
The plane crashed near a naval base, according to the presidency and the Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo.
Both described it as an ATR-42 -- a twin-engine turboprop that the manufacturers say can carry between 30 and 50 passengers
A video circulating on social media showed a small crowd gathered near a river while rescuers searched the area by boat.
The president said he had "directed the Nigerian Air Force to immediately commence a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to prevent future occurrences".
- Noise like thunder -
Dayo Akinte, a firewood hawker who lives about a kilometre from where the accident occurred, described to AFP hearing a sound she thought was "thunder" at the time she believed the plane went down.
Since the crash, "three aircraft have also been flying over the scene", she said by phone.
She said someone who went fishing in the swamp alerted the nearby naval base and people in the town about the crash.
Air Force spokesman Ehimen Ejodame earlier said "search and rescue operations" were ongoing "in coordination with relevant authorities and emergency response agencies".
Police also confirmed the accident but provided no details.
Igbokoda is located in Ilaje, an oil-producing region in southern Nigeria.
In May 2021, Nigeria's top-ranking army commander, Lieutenant General Ibrahim Attahiru, and 10 other officers were killed when their plane crashed in bad weather while trying to land at northern Kaduna state airport.
Seven people died when a military plane crashed into a house in northern Nigeria, killing everyone on board in August 2015.
Earlier that same month, a helicopter crashed into a lagoon in Lagos, killing six, including the American pilot.
- AFP

articles.title: ISA releases Inventory Of R395 Billion In Infrastructure Projects - Infrastructure News
articles.summary: ISA releases Inventory Of R395 Billion In Infrastructure Projects  Infrastructure News
articles.full_text:
Infrastructure South Africa’s third Construction Book identifies 110 projects worth R395bn across water, transport, energy, municipal and digital infrastructure.
Infrastructure South Africa (ISA) has released the third edition of the Construction Book, identifying 110 infrastructure projects with a combined value of approximately R395 billion and providing industry with greater visibility of projects expected to progress towards procurement and construction.
The Construction Book is intended to give contractors, professional service providers, suppliers, financiers and other industry participants a clearer view of the public-sector infrastructure pipeline over the next 12 to 18 months. Rather than simply providing a catalogue of projects, ISA positions the publication as a market-signalling tool designed to give companies sufficient lead time to plan capacity, skills, equipment, supply chains and partnerships.
The third edition has a national geographic spread and covers six infrastructure sectors. The largest component by value is municipal infrastructure, comprising 10 projects worth approximately R112 billion. The sector includes projects from municipalities including eThekwini, Cape Town, Polokwane, Tshwane, Johannesburg and Mogale City, reflecting the growing focus on infrastructure needed to support local economic development and essential services.
The publication also provides a more detailed view of the water and sanitation pipeline, with 18 projects valued at approximately R35 billion. These include dams, water treatment and wastewater treatment facilities, irrigation systems, reservoirs and pipelines. Among the projects highlighted are the Beitbridge Musina Water Transfer Scheme, the Southern Aqueduct in KwaZulu-Natal and the City of Cape Town’s proposed permanent desalination plant.
The Beitbridge Musina scheme, for example, involves approximately 20 km of pipeline crossing the Limpopo River between Beitbridge and Musina, with bidirectional capacity to transfer 41 Mℓ/day of treated water from the Beitbridge water treatment works to terminal reservoirs in Musina. The project is currently listed at feasibility stage, with procurement planned for the second quarter of 2027/28.
Transport accounts for 41 projects worth approximately R81 billion. The pipeline includes road, rail, logistics, airport and port projects, with significant activity from SANRAL, Transnet and major municipalities. Among the projects highlighted are upgrades to national road corridors, the modernisation of rail container corridors and the procurement of a new concessionaire to operate the Gautrain system.
The Construction Book notes a revival of rail and port investment through the Transnet group, with projects including the North-east, Cape, Central and Container corridors. These projects are aimed at restoring and expanding rail capacity and positioning the corridors for private-sector participation under the country’s rail reform programme.
Energy represents a further 29 projects with a combined value of approximately R86 billion. These include substations, power plants and transmission infrastructure, with the Aries-Aggenys 400 kV line in the Northern Cape and refurbishment of the main plant at Steenbras in the Western Cape among the projects identified by ISA.
Social infrastructure contributes 16 projects worth approximately R52 billion. The sector includes projects such as the Tygerberg and Belhar hospitals, Durban Film City, the Joburg Fresh Produce Market and Limpopo Central Hospital. ISA identifies social infrastructure as an area with significant potential for public-private partnerships, particularly because many projects have long-term operational requirements.
The third edition also introduces digital infrastructure as a distinct sector, with three projects valued at approximately R28 billion. These include investments associated with the MeerKAT radio astronomy project and the SAeX East Subsea Fibre-Optic Cable. The Construction Book describes digital infrastructure as an increasingly important component of economic and social development, encompassing fibre-optic networks, data centres, broadband and other communications infrastructure.
Greater role for PPPs
For the first time, the Construction Book specifically includes Public-Private Partnership projects. These span transport, social infrastructure, water and sanitation and reflect the government’s increasing use of alternative procurement and financing models to bring private-sector capital, expertise and operational capacity into infrastructure development.
The publication notes that the PPP Framework was revised with effect from June 2026, including a fast-track approval route for PPPs below R2 billion, greater delegated authority for accounting officers and strengthened technical oversight and project preparation. The revised framework also allows unsolicited private-sector bids for conceptual projects aligned with public-sector priorities.
The inclusion of PPPs is accompanied by a broader expansion of municipal infrastructure in the Construction Book. The previous edition profiled one municipality, while the latest edition includes multiple metropolitan and other municipalities. ISA describes municipal infrastructure as the largest sector in the publication by value, with projects intended to address infrastructure deficits while supporting service delivery and local economic activity.
From pipeline visibility to pipeline monitoring
Mameetse Masemola, Head of Infrastructure South Africa
The publication’s significance extends beyond identifying projects. ISA says it intends to introduce quarterly monitoring of projects included in the Construction Book, working with project sponsors to track procurement milestones, tenders issued, awards, construction commencement and material changes to project timelines, scope and value.
This is intended to provide a clearer picture of how projects move from planning and preparation into procurement and construction, while helping ISA identify recurring constraints and provide more timely information to industry.
Mameetse Masemola, Head of Infrastructure South Africa, says the objective is to create a clearer connection between the forward pipeline and the projects that ultimately enter the market.
“The Construction Book will complement, rather than replace, formal procurement platforms such as National Treasury’s eTender Portal. Our intention is to create a clearer line of sight between the forward infrastructure pipeline and the tenders that subsequently enter the market, enabling contractors, professional service providers, suppliers and financiers to plan and position themselves earlier.”
The Construction Book is therefore intended to provide information before projects reach formal tendering platforms, rather than serve as an alternative procurement mechanism. ISA says greater visibility should give companies time to prepare their capacity, secure equipment and skills, establish supply chains and position themselves for upcoming opportunities.
The third edition comes against a challenging backdrop for the construction sector. The Construction Book records construction employment at 1.42 million people at the end of 2025, while construction gross value added averaged R99 billion during 2025, below the R103.6 billion recorded in 2024. ISA identifies procurement delays, project preparation gaps, rising input costs, weak local government implementation capacity and disruptions on construction sites among the constraints affecting delivery.
Against this background, ISA’s approach places greater emphasis on the quality and maturity of the project pipeline, rather than simply the volume of projects announced.
The third edition comprises projects submitted by national and provincial departments, municipalities, state-owned entities and other implementing institutions. ISA says the publication will progressively become a more regular source of information on projects approaching the market, with monitoring intended to show whether projects are progressing as anticipated and where intervention may be required.
For an industry that needs to make investment and capacity decisions well ahead of construction activity, the value of the R395 billion pipeline will ultimately depend not only on the projects being listed, but on how effectively they move through preparation, procurement and into construction.

articles.title: Africa’s Global Power Paradox: 54 Nations, One Voice? - Independent Newspaper Nigeria
articles.summary: Africa’s Global Power Paradox: 54 Nations, One Voice?  Independent Newspaper Nigeria
articles.full_text:
Bolarinde Mathew Akinbinu
Africa has never had more reasons to speak with one voice. The continent has 54 countries, a population of about 1.5 billion people, some of the world’s fastest-growing consumer markets, vast agricultural potential, strategic energy resources and critical minerals increasingly central to the global economy. It also occupies an increasingly important position in the competition for investment, technology, energy security and geopolitical influence. Yet when African leaders speak on the international stage, a striking paradox emerges: they agree strongly on the need for greater African representation in global governance, but often disagree profoundly on how that influence should be achieved and which external partnerships should underpin it.
This paradox was particularly visible in the African interventions at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. Across the speeches examined, the demand for reform of the United Nations Security Council was one of the clearest areas of convergence. Nigeria called for at least two permanent African seats with the full rights and responsibilities of permanent membership, including veto rights for as long as the veto remains. Ghana argued that Africa’s exclusion from permanent membership is incompatible with the principle of sovereign equality. Mozambique similarly supported at least two permanent African seats, while Kenya, Namibia, Botswana, Somalia and other African representatives endorsed the broader African position on Security Council reform.
The substance of this demand is remarkably consistent. Africa contributes significantly to the United Nations system, participates in peacekeeping, carries a disproportionate share of the world’s development and security challenges, and represents the largest regional voting bloc in the General Assembly. Yet it remains without a permanent seat on the Security Council. The contradiction is difficult to ignore. African governments can therefore present a relatively unified position when the issue concerns institutional exclusion. The difficulty begins when the conversation moves from representation to power, security, financing and strategic alignment.
Nigeria’s intervention illustrates one version of the African response. Abuja does not advocate withdrawal from the existing international system. Instead, it calls for reform. Its position combines Security Council reform with stronger African integration, the African Continental Free Trade Area, industrialisation, technological development, climate finance, private capital and South-South cooperation. Nigeria also links continental security to cooperation against terrorism, organised crime, illicit finance and cross-border instability. Its message is essentially that Africa should acquire greater influence within a reformed multilateral system rather than abandon that system.
Ghana adopts a similarly Pan-African but more historically charged position. Its intervention connects contemporary economic inequality with the legacies of slavery, colonialism, resource extraction and unequal global finance. It argues that Africa should not remain an exporter of raw materials while value addition, industrial production and employment occur elsewhere. The reference to critical minerals is especially significant. Ghana’s message is that Africa’s lithium, cobalt, rare earths, gold and other strategic resources should not simply feed another global scramble for raw materials. Instead, the continent should process more of these resources domestically and capture a greater share of the value chain.
This is where geopolitics becomes inseparable from economics. The global transition towards electric vehicles, renewable energy, advanced batteries, semiconductors and other technologies has increased the strategic importance of minerals found in substantial quantities in Africa. For governments and businesses outside the continent, Africa represents an important source of future supply. For African governments, however, the strategic question is increasingly whether the continent will remain primarily an exporter of commodities or become a competitive location for processing, manufacturing and technology-intensive industries.
The difference is not simply philosophical. It has direct consequences for investment strategy. An African economy that exports unprocessed minerals captures one part of the value chain. An economy that develops refining, processing, component manufacturing, logistics, research and related services captures considerably more economic activity. This explains why industrialisation, infrastructure, energy supply, skills and intra-African trade appear repeatedly alongside demands for greater political representation.
Yet the continent’s economic ambitions are constrained by another major issue: finance. Several of the speeches express concern about the cost of borrowing, debt burdens, limited fiscal space and the structure of the international financial system. Ghana argues that developing countries often borrow at significantly higher costs than industrialised economies and calls for affordable concessional finance. Namibia highlights high borrowing costs, debt vulnerabilities and limited fiscal space. Kenya focuses on the cost of capital and the need for reforms that make international finance more responsive to developing economies. Mozambique calls for sustainable debt relief and greater access to predictable financing. Nigeria similarly calls for reform of the international financial architecture and wider access to concessional financing.
The language surrounding debt is becoming increasingly important in African political and economic discourse. African governments are not simply asking for more loans. They are questioning the terms under which capital is provided, the cost of servicing that capital and the extent to which debt obligations constrain spending on infrastructure, education, health and productive investment. Ghana’s intervention goes further by calling for climate finance that does not simply create additional debt burdens.
For international investors, this creates a paradox of its own. Africa requires substantial capital to develop infrastructure, energy systems, manufacturing capacity and digital networks, but high financing costs can undermine the commercial viability of precisely the investments needed to transform the continent’s productive structure. The challenge is therefore not merely attracting capital. It is creating financial conditions under which capital can support productive investment rather than deepen fiscal vulnerability.
The most profound division, however, concerns security and external partnerships. Here the African speeches reveal sharply different national calculations.
The Sahel provides the clearest example. Niger’s position is framed around sovereignty, independence and what it describes as a struggle against external domination. The speech explicitly invokes a “war of liberation” and argues that the country should determine its own security relationships, economic partnerships and use of natural resources. Russia and China are mentioned among the country’s external partners, alongside Algeria, Togo, Türkiye and Morocco.
Burkina Faso’s contribution to the Togo-Sahel Strategy meeting reinforces this sovereignty-centred narrative. Its foreign minister presents sovereignty in political, economic, security and cultural terms. Political sovereignty means choosing national leadership without external imposition. Economic sovereignty means ensuring that natural resources serve the population. Security sovereignty means determining where military equipment is purchased and where military personnel are trained. Cultural sovereignty means resisting externally imposed definitions of African identity and political legitimacy.
The Burkina Faso argument is particularly revealing because it does not advocate isolation. Rather, it seeks a different configuration of international relationships. Cooperation with China in the health sector is presented as evidence that alternative partnerships can deliver tangible development outcomes. The underlying proposition is that replacing dependence on one external partner with diversified partnerships constitutes an expression of sovereignty.
This approach contrasts with the position of countries whose security and development strategies remain deeply embedded in established international partnerships. Somalia, for example, emphasises the importance of international support for security, counterterrorism and institutional development. Mozambique acknowledges substantial security assistance from SADC, the European Union, Rwanda and Tanzania. The Central African Republic places significant emphasis on international peacekeeping and development support.
These differences cannot simply be described as ideological disagreement. They reflect materially different national circumstances. A country facing terrorism, insurgency or fragile institutions may have immediate security requirements that make international assistance indispensable. Another government may regard the same external security architecture as a constraint on sovereignty. Geography, domestic political history, economic structure and security threats therefore shape foreign policy in ways that make a single continental position difficult to sustain.
This is the central reason Africa’s geopolitical unity remains elusive. The continent has common interests, but its governments do not have identical interests.
Nigeria wants a stronger Africa within an effective multilateral system. Ghana wants reform of global institutions alongside greater economic justice and Pan-African industrialisation. Kenya seeks a more equitable global financial and trading system while remaining strongly engaged with international markets and institutions.
